newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala military police rebel, hold generals.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala military police rebel, hold generals.

text.p: About 400 armed military police locked two generals inside their fortified compound on Saturday after a breakdown of negotiations over the future of their army unit in peacetime Guatemala.

A third general was also briefly prevented from leaving in an escalation of a four-day rebellion by military police who are demanding the government pay them severance when they lose their jobs this year under the terms of a peace accord.

About 1,000 military police on Wednesday night defied their commanders and seized their compound in the first army rebellion against terms of the treaty signed Dec. 29 between the government and leftist rebels ending 36 years of civil war.
"We have been tricked. Don't let them out," yelled military police officers brandishing assault rifles from inside the compound on Saturday.
Police became agitated when negotiator Gen. Manuel Ventura told them the government needed more time to set severance terms. Police demanded an immediate response.

In a complete breakdown of military discipline inside the compound, police shouted and heckled the generals, physically surrounding them to prevent their departure, pushing them back inside with their weapons cocked.
Gen. Ventura was let go after promising to return to the compound later on Saturday with new proposals after meeting with government officials.
Presidential spokesman Ricardo de la Torre has labeled the uprising a "labor dispute," not an act of rebellion.
Military police have refused to report to work guarding banks and businesses in the capital during the protest.

The 4,000-strong military police (PMA) will be dissolved this year as part of government promises to leftist rebels. The peace accords do not specify what compensation the police will get when their jobs are eliminated.
The government pledged in the treaty to cut the armed forces by a third. The army has played a pivotal and at times, a brutal role in political life for much of Guatemala's recent history.

Police complain the guerrillas of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit had won a better deal in the peace accords than they did. International aid will provide job training and housing assistance for ex-rebels.
